title: Applied Anthropology and Culinary Arts

jokes.text: Professor Duncan responds to Shirley's answer about paleolithic hunting tribes: 'That's an interesting answer, miss Edison. Is it right? Don't know. Don't care. But so far, you're all getting As.'
jokes.setup: Shirley gives an earnest academic answer, expecting feedback on its correctness
jokes.punchline: Duncan has no idea and doesn't care — the entire class is a sham graded on vibes
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold open joke establishing Duncan's alcoholic negligence as a character trait. The pivot from academic formality to total indifference is sharp and sets up the whole episode's premise efficiently. High character integration because only Duncan's specific brand of boozy apathy makes this work.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Is this answer correct?

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: I don't know and I don't care. But you're getting an A anyway.

jokes.text: Annie protests that everyone getting As is unfair to people who studied. Duncan orders the class to throw paper balls at her head until she sits down.
jokes.setup: Annie, the conscientious student, raises a reasonable objection to grade inflation
jokes.punchline: The teacher responds by inciting the class to physically assault her into compliance
jokes.explanation: The joke weaponizes both characters perfectly: Annie's uptight earnestness and Duncan's degenerate authority. The escalation from 'that's unfair' to 'everyone throw things at her' is unexpected and proportionally absurd. Gets an 8 on impact because the room-incitement subverts the teacher-student dynamic so completely. Solid craft — it could only be this dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Professor, isn't it unfair that everyone gets an A?

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Well, if you have a problem with that, I could always just beat you.

jokes.text: Annie, pelted with paper balls: 'Oh! What? Oh.' then immediately: 'Sitting. I'm sitting.' Duncan: 'Good. Very good. A-pluses for all of you.'
jokes.setup: Annie is being physically coerced by her professor and classmates
jokes.punchline: She caves instantly and Duncan rewards the mob with A-pluses, completing the absurd transaction
jokes.explanation: The payoff to joke #2. Annie's immediate capitulation is funny on its own, but Duncan's approving 'Good. Very good.' as if she performed a trick, then upgrading everyone to A-pluses, extends the joke perfectly. The authority-figure-as-mob-boss dynamic lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Just throw paper at him.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: Sitting. I'm sitting.

jokes.text: Abed or Troy tells Duncan he's a great teacher 'when you're drinking.' Duncan thanks him, calling him 'Darrell.' The student corrects him: 'It's Troy.'
jokes.setup: A student compliments Duncan warmly on his teaching ability
jokes.punchline: Duncan doesn't even know his name despite giving him an A
jokes.explanation: Classic 'teacher doesn't know student's name' joke elevated by the specific context: Duncan is celebrating with these students while awarding them grades. The disconnect between the warmth of the compliment and Duncan's total ignorance is well-executed in just a few words.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Darrell, could you help me with this?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's Troy, actually.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Let him call you Darrell. Duncan's about to give Darrell an A.

jokes.text: Jeff or another student responds to the name confusion: 'Hey, the man wants to give Darrell an A, let him do it.'
jokes.setup: Troy corrects Duncan on his name
jokes.punchline: Jeff pragmatically defends the wrong name because the grade outcome is the same
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-serving pragmatism is core to his character — he immediately calculates that correcting Duncan isn't worth it if the A stays. The joke is small but efficient and character-consistent. 'Let him do it' is the right level of lazy cynicism.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: To pathetic.

jokes.text: Duncan raises a toast: 'To the easiest school, the dumbest dean...' [cut] 'And the ultimate blow off class. Anthropology. Who knew?'
jokes.setup: A toast at what appears to be an academic setting
jokes.punchline: Duncan toasts to the worthlessness of everything he's supposed to represent, with genuine enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: The toast structure creates a comedic runway — we know something transgressive is coming when Duncan starts. 'The dumbest dean' works because it's specific institutional mockery in front of a journalist. 'Who knew?' lands as a genuine expression of Duncan's self-awareness about his own uselessness.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's fine if it's my baby. Chang babies love alcohol and duck.

jokes.text: Chang to pregnant Shirley: 'Well, if it's my child, it's okay to have a drink or two. Chang babies love the sauce, you know? Alcohol and duck.'
jokes.setup: Shirley explains she's not drinking because she's pregnant
jokes.punchline: Chang claims potential paternity and immediately prescribes prenatal alcohol and duck as Chang baby nutrition
jokes.explanation: The 'alcohol and duck' specificity is what elevates this. It's not just Chang being irresponsible — there's a whole implied Chang cultural mythology baked into two words. Character integration is very high: only Chang would claim potential paternity and immediately use it as a loophole to prescribe fetal alcohol syndrome. The duck addition is perfectly absurd and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: How do you know the baby isn't mine?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Because when Chang's baby is born, the seas will turn to blood, the locusts will darken the sky, and a great wailing will echo across the land.

jokes.text: Shirley insists it's Andre's baby: 'Because I don't see any locusts.' Pause. 'Besides, a woman knows these things.'
jokes.setup: Chang demands to know how Shirley knows the baby isn't his
jokes.punchline: Shirley cites the absence of locusts as evidence, then backtracks to 'a woman knows things' as if that's a more reasonable explanation
jokes.explanation: Exceptional comedic writing. The locust line works on multiple levels: it implies a Chang birth is a biblical plague event, it's completely absurd, and Shirley delivers it with the confidence of citing actual evidence before remembering she should use a more rational excuse. The beat where she pivots to 'a woman knows these things' is perfect — the locusts line was clearly more convincing to her too. Easily an 8+ moment.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Women are so connected to their bodies, you know? It's like we're one with ourselves.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Britta, you have a booger.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's part of me.

jokes.text: In the middle of a philosophical discussion about women's connection to their bodies, Chang says 'You have a booger.' Shirley: 'I know. It's part of me.'
jokes.setup: Shirley is delivering a speech about women's embodied knowledge and connectedness
jokes.punchline: Chang punctures the speech by pointing out a booger; Shirley absorbs the information and re-integrates it into her argument without missing a beat
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: Shirley's philosophical speech about embodied female knowledge is immediately undercut by a booger observation, but instead of being embarrassed, she incorporates it into her thesis ('I know. It's part of me.'). It's a perfect two-line exchange — economy is exceptional, it couldn't be funnier with more words. It's character-specific (Shirley's dignity absorbs everything), surprising, and deeply quotable. Approaches the 8+ benchmark clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Alright, everyone, settle down. This is a serious exam. Question one: 'This class is fake. Discuss.'

jokes.text: Toast: 'Here is to never telling the dean.'
jokes.setup: The class is celebrating their fraudulent easy A
jokes.punchline: The toast reveals they're actively hiding their academic fraud from the dean — who is about to walk in
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony setup — the audience knows or suspects the dean is about to arrive. Functional and efficient but fairly standard sitcom mechanism.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: In many cultures, the breaking of the glass represents the fragility of life and the solemnity of the marriage contract. Among Jewish traditions, this practice symbolizes the destruction of the Temple and—

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Why are you all looking at me like that? I'm simply explaining the anthropological significance of—oh. Oh no. This is a baby shower, isn't it?

jokes.text: Duncan mid-toast: '...And that is what Jews do at weddings.'
jokes.setup: We cut into a toast already in progress; we have no idea what Duncan was explaining
jokes.punchline: The punchline of whatever story he was telling is delivered completely out of context, implying a bizarre and tangential digression during a final exam
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy — the entire joke is delivered mid-scene as a cut-to, and the humor is entirely in what we didn't hear. The specificity of 'Jews at weddings' as the conclusion of an unseen story is funnier than anything the story itself could have been. Community's willingness to leave the audience to imagine the worst is good craft.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I'm a father figure to these students. My educational approach creates that dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Though I suppose that makes me less like a father and more like the parents in 'Children of the Corn.'

jokes.text: The Dean introduces himself to a journalist as 'a father figure to the kids' with an 'outside the box approach to education' — 'like that film Children of the Corn.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is puffing himself up for a journalist from Dean Magazine
jokes.punchline: His example of innovative fatherly education is a horror film about murderous children
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dean Pelton joke. He's so self-aggrandizing that he reaches for a cinematic reference to validate himself without processing that Children of the Corn is a horror film about children murdering adults. The gap between his intent and his example is the joke, and it's entirely character-specific. 'Oh, professor. What?' reaction beat makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Well, as you can see, this is a comprehensive examination. We have the written portion here, the oral component, and of course, the interpretive clay sculpture section.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: It really separates the wheat from the chaff. The clay doesn't lie.

jokes.text: Duncan realizes mid-class he's left the exam in his office. He then pivots immediately to promising 'a lump of clay' as an 'interactive element' and 'performance component.'
jokes.setup: Duncan is supposed to administer a final exam
jokes.punchline: He forgot it, then improvises increasingly grandiose academic language ('interactive element,' 'performance component') to dress up the fact that he's about to give everyone clay
jokes.explanation: Duncan's ability to dress up failure in academic jargon is a core character bit. 'I don't want to tip it, but there may be a lump of clay coming to everyone' is a funny line because of the buildup of pedagogical language preceding the reveal. 'Toodle-oo. Cheerio.' exit seals it.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Wow, this is real college.

jokes.text: Duncan exits with 'Toodle-oo. Cheerio.' and the journalist marvels: 'Wowee. This is a real college.'
jokes.setup: Duncan has just revealed his exam plan is a lump of clay and scurried out
jokes.punchline: The journalist, who is there to document educational excellence, is impressed
jokes.explanation: 'Wowee. This is a real college.' is a great deadpan line — the journalist's reverence is proportionally absurd given what just happened. It's short, well-placed, and the word 'wowee' is doing a lot of character work for someone supposedly from a magazine.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So you got your Mexican food trucks, your Korean BBQ trucks, your Thai trucks...

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know, I love how we all come together through food. It doesn't matter what color you are.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I mean, not that there's anything wrong with color. Colors are great. All colors.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm not saying some colors are better than other colors. That would be racist.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I love every color equally. Even the colors that— you know what, I'm just gonna stop talking.

jokes.text: Jeff pitches the World Food Festival: 'There are lunch trucks with 18 different nationalities of food.' Then immediately corrects himself: 'You know what, not different. Equal. Equal to whites. You know what, better than whites.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is enthusiastically describing the food festival
jokes.punchline: He catches himself using language that sounds dismissive of non-white food, over-corrects in real time, and overshoots into the opposite direction — all in one breath
jokes.explanation: Smart social-awkwardness comedy. Jeff's real-time self-correction that overshoots is very true to liberal guilt and the show's satirical voice. The escalation from 'different' to 'equal to whites' to 'better than whites' in rapid succession is well-structured. Character-specific because Jeff is exactly the kind of guy who would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: One of them was so late, he came out with a driver's license!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I'm joking.

jokes.text: Shirley claims her discomfort is 'just indigestion' and says her other two kids came 'right on schedule.' 'Jordan was in here so long, he came out with a driver's license. I'm kidding. That's not true.'
jokes.setup: Shirley is insisting she's not in labor, recounting her previous normal pregnancies
jokes.punchline: The hyperbolic driver's license line, followed immediately by her own disclaimer
jokes.explanation: The self-correction after a hyperbolic joke ('I'm kidding. That's not true.') is a Shirley verbal signature — she makes an outrageous claim and then walks it back with prim clarity. It's a very specific comedic tic that's character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Chang babies are parasitic creatures that eat their mothers from the inside out.

jokes.text: Chang explains Chang gestation: 'We gestate fast because we're better at obtaining nutrients. Some need only eight months, depending on how much of the mother they eat.'
jokes.setup: Chang is claiming Chang babies are always premature due to superior biology
jokes.punchline: The explanation escalates to Chang fetuses eating their mothers from the inside
jokes.explanation: Chang's mythology about Chang babies is some of the best running material in this episode. 'Depending on how much of the mother they eat' is a perfect dark escalation delivered with complete sincerity. The building of an absurd internal logic around Chang genetics is excellent character work — it's not random, it's consistent with Chang's grandiose self-mythology.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Big Antacid doesn't want you to know this, but antacids are a government conspiracy to keep your digestive system dependent on pharmaceutical companies.

jokes.text: Britta warns Shirley that antacid is 'full of chemicals' and suggests she take eucalyptus root and pig saliva instead, citing that it's 'the same active ingredient as antacid. They just dress it up with a fancy name.'
jokes.setup: Shirley tries to take antacid for her discomfort
jokes.punchline: Britta's alternative (pig saliva) is demonstrably more disgusting and questionable than antacid, while she treats antacid as the dangerous option. 'They just dress it up with a fancy name' — the name being 'antacid'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Britta character joke. Her 'Big Antacid' conspiracy thinking, combined with recommending pig saliva as the natural alternative, is exactly her brand of well-intentioned but backwards activism. Character integration is near-perfect — this joke is entirely Britta. 'How dare they' from Shirley is a nice topper.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, are you trying to pull an Indecent Proposal on us?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He's offering money for something precious and intimate.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? No! It's just a handshake!

jokes.text: Shirley responds to Britta's Big Antacid conspiracy: 'How dare they.'
jokes.setup: Britta has explained that antacid is a corporate cover for pig saliva
jokes.punchline: Shirley responds with flat, genuine indignation — she's bought it
jokes.explanation: Three words that extend the previous joke beautifully. Shirley immediately accepting Britta's pseudoscience is funny because it undercuts her earlier assertion that she's smarter than Chang's nonsense. Good economy, decent character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: ...I don't know.

jokes.text: Troy and Abed's secret handshake — they perform it when one of them 'says something awesome.' Jeff wants in and offers $1,000.
jokes.setup: Jeff notices Troy and Abed do a handshake and asks why
jokes.punchline: The 'rule' is completely arbitrary ('I don't know, it just is'), and Jeff's response is to immediately try to buy his way in for $1,000
jokes.explanation: Setup for the episode's B-plot. Troy and Abed's bond being expressed through unexplainable in-group rituals is very true to their characters, and Jeff's immediate impulse to monetize it rather than earn it is perfect Jeff. The $1,000 offer is a funny escalation — he could just ask nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: The epidural is the only socially acceptable way for me to get high.

jokes.text: Pierce is offered the handshake deal instead. He and Jeff roleplay Indecent Proposal: 'Indecent Proposal. Indecent Proposal.' / 'Woody.' / 'Demi.'
jokes.setup: Jeff offers $1,000 to get the handshake; Pierce apparently intercepts the transaction
jokes.punchline: Pierce and Jeff immediately lean into an Indecent Proposal bit, assigning each other roles, suggesting this is a weirdly natural dynamic for them
jokes.explanation: The reference works because Pierce is the right age to reach for Indecent Proposal and Jeff's willingness to play along (calling himself 'Woody') is funny in its implication. It's not a great joke on its own but the specificity of the reference in context is decent.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Some women have orgasms during natural birth.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Britta! Oh my God, we are talking about my baby!

jokes.text: After the Indecent Proposal bit, someone asks 'You two gonna fall in love?' Troy: 'No.' Abed: 'I don't know.'
jokes.setup: The Indecent Proposal roleplay implies a quasi-romantic transaction between Jeff and Pierce
jokes.punchline: The question is redirected to Troy and Abed's relationship, and Abed's uncertainty is quietly telling
jokes.explanation: Abed's 'I don't know' is a lovely small moment — it's both funny and emotionally interesting given the Troy-Abed dynamic. The economy is excellent (two words containing multitudes). It's a blink-and-miss-it gem that rewards attention.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Two one-eyed cats? That's depressing.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: They're not depressing! Together they have perfect vision. It's actually beautiful.

jokes.text: Britta hints that some women achieve orgasm during natural childbirth ('...some women can actually achieve or--'). Shirley cuts her off: 'That's not something a woman does on her child's head.'
jokes.setup: Britta is citing an article about the natural endorphin rush of chemical-free childbirth
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately understands where Britta is going and shuts it down with specific moral framing: not the act itself, but the location relative to the child
jokes.explanation: Shirley's specific objection — not 'that's disgusting' but 'not on her child's head' — is brilliantly specific. It implies she has thought about this in detail and has fine-grained moral rules. The specificity is what makes it exceptional. Character integration is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you're gonna have the baby naturally? What, are you gonna squat in a field like a pioneer woman while your one-eyed cats half watch?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: My cats aren't one-eyed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Not yet.

jokes.text: Annie rips into Britta: 'Listen, backseat birther, Shirley's on her third kid. She doesn't need a third-year-old slacker with two one-eyed cats governing her body.'
jokes.setup: Britta has been lecturing Shirley on natural childbirth against her wishes
jokes.punchline: Annie's takedown invents 'backseat birther,' establishes Britta's specific life circumstances (slacker, two one-eyed cats) as disqualifying credentials, and pins the argument on bodily autonomy
jokes.explanation: 'Backseat birther' alone is a great coinage. The specific detail of 'two one-eyed cats' as Britta's credentialing failure is excellent — it's not just 'you have no experience,' it's 'you have two half-blind cats.' This is Annie unleashed, and her sudden viciousness is both funny and character-revealing. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh no, what if I give birth right here in the classroom?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Star-Burns would be the first thing my baby sees. I can't let that happen!

jokes.text: Britta responds to 'two one-eyed cats': 'First of all, together, my cats can do anything.'
jokes.setup: Annie has used Britta's two one-eyed cats as evidence of her incompetence
jokes.punchline: Britta's first priority is to defend the cats' combined capabilities
jokes.explanation: Perfect. Britta's priorities are exposed: she responds to a multi-pronged attack by first defending the cats' combined visual coverage. 'Together, my cats can do anything' is a genuinely great line — it's absurd, it's specific, it's delivered with Britta's characteristic defensive sincerity, and it's immediately quotable. Economy is exceptional — nine words that tell you everything about Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: I'll drive you to the hospital! My car's right outside. It's a 2004 Nissan Sentra.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Dean, I'm in labor.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: But it has a very fuel-efficient engine. And the interior is surprisingly spacious.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Secondly, you disqualified yourself from this conversation the moment you decided to grow a wang.' Jeff: 'I regret nothing.'
jokes.setup: Britta is defending herself from Annie's attack and realizes Jeff is also weighing in
jokes.punchline: She dismisses Jeff with a gender-based disqualification; Jeff's reply ('I regret nothing') is funny because he had no apparent agency in the matter
jokes.explanation: 'I regret nothing' in response to 'you decided to grow a wang' is a funny beat because it treats biological inevitability as a proud personal choice. Decent joke, elevated by delivery context.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Can somebody call Andre?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What? Andre gets a cute nickname and I don't?

jokes.text: Annie fires back at Britta: imagining her 'squatting in a babbling brook' while 'a beautiful star child slides out on a ray of sunshine while your cats each half watch because you're so natural.'
jokes.setup: Annie is mocking Britta's natural birth ideology
jokes.punchline: The image escalates to full hippie parody: babbling brook, star child, ray of sunshine — and the cats each only watching with one eye as the capstone callback
jokes.explanation: Annie's escalating parody of natural birth reaches a fever pitch with the brook/star child/sunshine imagery, and the callback to the one-eyed cats ('each half watch') is a perfect button. The cats 'each half watching' is a great image — returning to the earlier joke and extending its logic. Annie's ferocity in this whole sequence is a character revelation.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We can never have a normal class experience. It's always something with this group. One time we had a paintball war, another time we turned a blanket fort into an actual situation, and don't even get me started on the time we investigated a conspiracy that turned out to be about nothing. A normal day of learning is like asking for world peace at Greendale.

jokes.text: Shirley's water breaks mid-argument. Someone asks for 'every mop on campus.'
jokes.setup: The argument about natural vs. medical childbirth is reaching its peak
jokes.punchline: Shirley's water breaks immediately after, the universe answering the debate with action
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom timing — the argument about childbirth philosophy is immediately answered by real childbirth. 'Can someone please get every mop on campus' is the perfect prosaic response to an emergency. The request for every mop (not some mops, every mop) is a small but effective comedic exaggeration.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: This must be my baby. I was at the hospital that night.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, I was near a hospital. Okay, I was in a hospital parking lot.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Fine, I was at a Duane Reade across the street from a hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Look, I was on a treadmill at a gym. And not just any gym—a gym that was in the same city as a hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: The treadmill was on the third floor. The one by the window. The one that's always broken but I fixed it myself with a screwdriver and some duct tape I found in the lost and found.

jokes.text: Chang's immediate reaction: 'Chang baby!' followed by someone asking 'Did you break water? Is that broken water? That's broken water!'
jokes.setup: Shirley's water breaks
jokes.punchline: Chang immediately claims the baby as his own; someone else processes the situation through increasingly confirming questions
jokes.explanation: Chang's triumphant 'Chang baby!' is consistent with his ongoing claims. The escalating 'broken water' question is a funny reaction beat — someone processing an emergency through confirmation loops.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: There are so many Changs in the world that I'm completely ungoogleable. You google 'Chang' and you get 47 million results. You google 'Kevin Durant' and you get Kevin Durant. You google me and you get a guy in Taiwan who sells DVDs out of his trunk.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Oh, father, God almighty, this isn't happening. It's too soon. I don't want my baby's first memory to be star-burns.'
jokes.setup: Shirley is in labor and panicking about giving birth in the classroom
jokes.punchline: Among all her legitimate fears, her specific concern is that Star-Burns is present
jokes.explanation: Star-Burns as an ambient figure in the Greendale universe is well-established, and the idea that his sideburns would be a baby's first trauma is very funny. 'I don't want my baby's first memory to be Star-Burns' is a specific, quotable, well-calibrated line. It tells you everything about how both Shirley and the community view Star-Burns.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'll give you a thousand dollars for that handshake.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's right. One thousand dollars. You know what that means? A thousand dollar handshake. You'll be shaking hands at a thousand dollars a pop. It'll be like... it'll be like the year 2000, but with money. Year 2-dollar sign-thousand.

jokes.text: The Dean offers to get his Prius, then mid-crisis says: 'I drive a Prius, which I think is pretty cool.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is trying to organize an emergency response to Shirley going into labor
jokes.punchline: He interrupts his own crisis management to self-promote his hybrid car ownership
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dean Pelton joke. In the middle of a genuine emergency, he cannot resist a small piece of personal branding. 'Which I think is pretty cool' — not 'which is very fuel efficient' or any practical justification, but an opinion about coolness — is exactly his brand of narcissistic insecurity. Character integration is excellent; this joke couldn't belong to anyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Betty Grable!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not how this works, Pierce.

jokes.text: Troy and Abed react to the chaos: 'We came so close to having one class that wasn't all about them.' / 'Remember when they all took that fishing trip on St. Patrick's Day? God, that was a good week.'
jokes.setup: The group has once again made a class all about themselves
jokes.punchline: Troy and Abed nostalgically remember a week when the main characters were absent — implying they prefer life without them
jokes.explanation: A clever meta-joke about ensemble sitcom dynamics — the supporting characters have an opinion about the leads. The specificity of a fishing trip on St. Patrick's Day (a week the audience didn't see, so presumably uneventful in the best possible way) is funny. It's a rare moment of minor characters having interiority.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what? Fine. You're a prostitute.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Now do the handshake.

jokes.text: Chang explains the Chang baby birthing mythology: 'More like taxicabs, hardware stores, bank lines, sewers. My nephew Jin was born on a treadmill at Bally Total Fitness. 20% incline.'
jokes.setup: Chang insists this is definitely a Chang baby and that Changs are never born in hospitals
jokes.punchline: He provides an escalating list of inappropriate birth locations, capping with the specific detail of a 20% treadmill incline
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of Chang birth locations is very strong comedy writing — 'taxicabs, hardware stores, bank lines, sewers' is already a great escalation, but the nephew on a treadmill with the specific incline percentage is the perfect button. '20% incline' is doing enormous comedic work — it's the detail that makes the whole thing feel real. This is an 8+ joke.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Who's Betty Grable?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's all I wanted.

jokes.text: Chang: 'Hey, show me some respect. I might be that child's estranged father.'
jokes.setup: Someone tries to manage Chang during the emergency
jokes.punchline: Chang demands respect on the grounds that he might be an estranged father — using 'estranged' as if it's an honorific
jokes.explanation: Chang pre-labeling himself as 'estranged' before the baby is even born is very funny — he's already written the narrative of his absentee fatherhood. Character-specific and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: This is better than dog dollars.

jokes.text: Pierce tries to buy the Troy/Abed handshake in the middle of the labor emergency. Jeff: 'Pierce, we're about to take Shirley to the hospital. This is not the time.' Pierce: 'Oh, it's the time. According to my watch, it's 1,000 o'clock.'
jokes.setup: Jeff tells Pierce this is not the time to negotiate
jokes.punchline: Pierce refutes this with a specific reading from his watch: 1,000 o'clock
jokes.explanation: 'According to my watch, it's 1,000 o'clock' is an excellent line. It has the structure of a real rebuttal (consulting a watch for authority) with completely nonsensical content. It's also very Pierce — he's the kind of man who would own a watch that says 1,000 o'clock and treat it as an argument. High quotability; this is a line that lands outside of context too.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It was easy! I just walked in there and said, 'I want to buy your handshake.' They said, 'Okay.' I gave them money. Done.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You can't just buy a handshake, Pierce! That's not how it works!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: A handshake is sacred. It's a bond between two people. It means something.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You just... you just destroyed something pure.

jokes.text: Pierce buys the handshake. Troy and Abed teach it to him. Pierce tries 'Betty Grable' and waits expectantly. Nothing happens. 'I said Betty Grable.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has bought the rights to the handshake and is told it activates when someone 'says something awesome'
jokes.punchline: Pierce says 'Betty Grable' — clearly thinking it's impressive — and Troy and Abed don't react, because it isn't awesome to them
jokes.explanation: The handshake B-plot pays off beautifully here. 'Betty Grable' is funny as Pierce's chosen 'awesome' thing — it's a 1940s pin-up star, the kind of reference that would impress his generation, completely meaningless to Troy and Abed. The extended silence after 'I said Betty Grable' (inferring the awkward pause from the timestamp gap at 08:40) makes this a prolonged cringe moment. Excellent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: See, this is what happens. We create something pure, something real, and then the second it has any value, the machine moves in and commodifies it. Flattens it. Makes it safe for mass consumption.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The handshake was ours. It meant something. And now it's just another product placement opportunity, another demographic target.

jokes.text: Jeff/someone tells Troy to 'Make your money, whore' to get him to do the handshake with Pierce.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed are holding out against Pierce's purchased handshake demand
jokes.punchline: The blunt transactional language ('make your money, whore') frames the handshake as sex work, which makes the entire subplot suddenly very dark
jokes.explanation: Four words that reframe the entire B-plot with maximum efficiency. The implication is delightfully dark and quotable. This kind of sudden tonal shift is one of Community's signature moves.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You two are like Rosemary's Baby, except the baby is stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: What does that even mean?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It's a 1968 Roman Polanski film about a woman who believes her unborn child is the spawn of Satan. Mia Farrow gives a career-defining performance, and the cinematography perfectly captures the paranoia of—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Pierce, you just called us stupid.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I know what I said. Now, as I was saying, the film's exploration of motherhood and isolation remains a masterpiece of psychological horror that modern filmmakers could only dream of replicating.

jokes.text: After the handshake happens with Pierce, Pierce asks: 'Who's Betty Grable?' Troy and Abed react with 'Yeah, that's the stuff.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has been demanding the handshake on the basis of saying 'Betty Grable,' which he presented as impressive
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he has no idea who Betty Grable is — the reference was bluffed
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff. Pierce went to the mat demanding a handshake for saying 'Betty Grable,' withstanding the entire standoff — only to immediately reveal he was name-dropping without knowledge. It retroactively makes every moment of his determination funnier. 'Yeah, that's the stuff' from Troy/Abed is exactly the right reaction — not explaining who Betty Grable is, just savoring the confirmation that Pierce is completely out of his depth. This is excellent comedy architecture. Easily an 8-9 range joke.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: This is blood money. Pierce's blood money.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We had something special. A magic that can never be recaptured.

jokes.text: Abed gives medical assessment of Shirley's labor while the handshake drama is happening: 'Her contractions are still six minutes apart. So unless her cervix is dilated more than eight centimeters, we still have time to get her to a hospital.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is exasperated that people are arguing about a handshake while Shirley is in labor
jokes.punchline: Abed has been quietly monitoring Shirley's cervical dilation while the other drama unfolded, and reports it clinically
jokes.explanation: Abed's ability to process emergency medical information as background data while the foreground is a handshake dispute is perfectly in character. His matter-of-fact cervical dilation update is funny precisely because of the contrast. Only Abed would have been monitoring this.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You guys realize a baby was just born, right? That's the actual miracle happening here.

jokes.text: Troy: 'Money doesn't matter anymore. Once you've sold something out, you can't get it back.' Pierce: 'You two are dumber than Jackie Coogan.'
jokes.setup: Troy makes a sincere statement about the loss of the handshake's meaning
jokes.punchline: Pierce deflates the pathos with a reference to Jackie Coogan (the child actor who was famously exploited for his earnings) — an oddly specific and historically relevant insult that also applies to Troy literally selling something
jokes.explanation: Pierce's Jackie Coogan reference is both surprisingly apt (a child star who had his earnings taken by adults) and very Pierce — his random old Hollywood references. The fact that it's explained in the next joke makes it a setup that rewards patient viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, where were you when this happened?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Off in the background. You know, like how you're not always the center of every story?

jokes.text: Pierce: 'He divorced Betty Grable.' — the callback that explains why Pierce knew the name
jokes.setup: Pierce insulted Troy by referencing Jackie Coogan; now it's revealed WHY Pierce knew Betty Grable — she was Coogan's ex-wife
jokes.punchline: Pierce's obscure old Hollywood knowledge has an internal logic — he knew Betty Grable as Jackie Coogan's ex — which retroactively makes his earlier repeated use of 'Betty Grable' even funnier
jokes.explanation: This is the best structural joke in the episode. In four words, Pierce's character is deepened AND the entire Betty Grable sequence is recontextualized. Pierce isn't random — he has an internal reference library of Old Hollywood that he thought everyone shared. 'He divorced Betty Grable' explains everything that came before in retrospect. This is craft-forward comedy writing at its best — economy (four words), structure (perfect callback payoff), character integration (completely Pierce), and originality (who else would construct a joke this way?). Genuinely exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Look, what happened at the food festival was more of a... kerfuffle than a full-scale... you know.

jokes.text: Abed: 'I delivered a baby earlier this year in the back of an SUV.' Jeff: 'What? Where was I when that happened?' Abed: 'I don't know. Off in the background.'
jokes.setup: Abed reveals he has relevant experience with emergency births
jokes.punchline: Jeff's absence from that event is explained as him being 'off in the background' — a sly reference to how secondary characters exist in ensemble TV
jokes.explanation: The meta joke about characters existing 'in the background' while the main plot happens elsewhere is elegant — it comments on ensemble TV storytelling while also being a funny dismissal of Jeff's ego. Abed is the right character to deliver it because his self-awareness about narrative structure is core to who he is. Solid 8-range joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The Korean War was a conflict between... well, it was about territory and ideology, but also—you know what, the real tragedy is that nobody talks about it. It's like the forgotten war. Unlike World War II, which everyone knows about, Korea just gets swept under the rug, kind of like how we sweep up the kimchi after these food fights...

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: And frankly, some of those Korean tactics were pretty brutal. I mean, not that I'm comparing them to anyone specific, but if you really think about it, the whole thing was a mess of—wait, is this being recorded?

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Everything is recorded, Dean.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh God.

jokes.text: The Dean explains that the World Food Festival has 'turned into a bit of a race...' and then corrects himself: 'Kerfuffle.' Jeff: 'You mean riot?' Dean: 'Let's use kerfuffle for now, okay, Mr. Winger?'
jokes.setup: The Dean is describing a food festival that has apparently descended into ethnic violence
jokes.punchline: He catches himself before saying 'riot' (or 'race riot'), replaces it with 'kerfuffle,' and then insists on the euphemism as PR management — with a journalist present
jokes.explanation: The 'kerfuffle' substitution for a race riot, in front of a Dean Magazine journalist, is an excellent Dean Pelton joke. His institutional damage-control instinct overrides his ability to respond to an emergency. 'Let's use kerfuffle for now' implies it's only a kerfuffle until the article is published. Character-specific and smart.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Shirley, I have some bad news.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh no, what is it?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Just imagine I'm saying this with a lot of emotion, because I can't actually do that.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton, defending the food festival chaos: 'I was just trying to feed hungry foodies.'
jokes.setup: A race riot has broken out at the Dean's World Food Festival
jokes.punchline: His self-defense reduces a riot to a simple act of feeding foodies — with 'foodies' doing significant unintentional ironic work
jokes.explanation: 'Feed hungry foodies' is a great small line. The word 'foodies' is incongruous with a riot and makes the Dean's well-meaning incompetence clear. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: If this baby is mine, listen to me. You must paint the nursery walls with the tears of a weeping willow.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: And the crib must face magnetic north, or the baby will be born with a crooked aura.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You cannot whistle on Tuesdays. Not even humming. Humming is a whistle's cousin.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Feed the baby only food that has been blessed by a man named Gerald. There are seventeen Geralds in the phone book. You'll know which one when you call.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: And most importantly, on the baby's first birthday, you must release seven lottery-winning rabbits into the forest while chanting in Aramaic.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton: 'I mean, I didn't even know there was a difference between North and South Korean barbecue. I mean, M*A*S*H lasted longer than that war. Get over it. Am I right? Don't print that.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is trying to explain how the ethnic food riot started
jokes.punchline: He casually dismisses Korean geopolitics using a TV show's run length as historical context, then realizes the journalist is present
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dean Pelton lines in the episode. 'M*A*S*H lasted longer than that war. Get over it.' is brilliantly stupid — measuring historical trauma against a TV show's runtime is the exact kind of oblivious privilege the Dean embodies. 'Don't print that' is the perfect button — his self-awareness arrives immediately after the damage. The specificity of M*A*S*H makes this exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I need someone to check my cervix dilation.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'll do it! I'm really good at looking at things.

jokes.text: Jeff reports: '911 says it's gonna take over an hour because of a race kerfuffle.' Dean: 'Oh. Lake Woebegone. Eeh!'
jokes.setup: An ambulance can't reach them because of the riot
jokes.punchline: The Dean responds to this emergency with 'Lake Woebegone' and a grimace — a completely non-sequitur public radio reference as a placeholder for distress
jokes.explanation: The Dean responding to a crisis with a reference to a gentle public radio program ('Lake Wobegon') is consistent with his character — his reference points are off and his emotional responses are mismatched. Decent absurdist beat.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I've delivered babies before. Well, not delivered, but I was present for the conception of at least two of them.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Don't worry, I'm a pro. Just like my boy Rob Lowe, I'm here to help you with the... with the... glow? No, the flow! The birth flow, that rhymes with Rob Lowe.

jokes.text: Chang insists that for a proper Chang birth, Shirley must elevate her legs over her head facing northeast, not look at the door ('bad luck'), and visualize 'a rabbit riding a dragon' to increase the baby's lottery chances.
jokes.setup: Abed has told Shirley they won't make it to the hospital
jokes.punchline: Chang's alternative birthing guidance is an escalating list of superstitious nonsense with specific, internally consistent logic
jokes.explanation: More excellent Chang mythology. The 'rabbit riding a dragon' detail to increase lottery-winning odds is the perfect absurdist capstone — it's not health-related at all, it's about financial luck, which reveals Chang's real priorities. The northeast-facing, door-avoidance, lottery visualization package is a coherent if insane belief system. Very strong character work.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I can check your dilation. I've done this before.

jokes.text: Chang: 'Also if you can visualize a rabbit riding a dragon, it'll increase his chances of winning lotteries.'
jokes.setup: Chang is continuing his list of Chang birth superstitions
jokes.punchline: The rabbit-riding-dragon visualization as a lottery-winning technique applied to a baby being born is both culturally absurdist and completely specific
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the Chang superstition bit. The lottery-winning goal for a newborn is an absurdly practical aspiration, and the specific image of a rabbit on a dragon is funny in its specificity. 'Lotteries' (plural) suggests serious ambitions for the child.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You just realized you've been pronouncing 'gif' wrong your whole life, didn't you?

jokes.text: Annie agrees to examine Shirley and says: 'No problowe, Rob Lowe.'
jokes.setup: Annie is told what to do and agrees
jokes.punchline: Annie's agreement is delivered as a rhyming catchphrase with a celebrity name that makes no particular sense in context
jokes.explanation: A charming absurdist rhyming agreement — 'No problowe, Rob Lowe' has good rhythm and is a funny way for Annie to handle her nervousness. The Rob Lowe name-drop has no context, which is part of the joke. It's a minor moment but a fun one.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Are many babies born in classrooms?

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Well, more are conceived there.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: I mean, not— that's not what I meant. Though, statistically speaking, it's sort of true.

jokes.text: Annie's reaction upon seeing Shirley's situation — the transcript shows a music beat [13:09] followed by Abed's dry: 'I take it the head has reached the cervix.'
jokes.setup: Annie looks to assess how far along Shirley is
jokes.punchline: The wordless horrified reaction from Annie (inferred from the beat and Abed's reading of it) is the joke; Abed's calm diagnostic deduction is the button
jokes.explanation: Classic visual comedy where the transcript points to a performance moment: Annie's reaction is so clear from her face that Abed can deduce the answer without being told. 'I take it the head has reached the cervix' is a brilliantly deadpan Abed line — it treats a visceral human moment as an equation to be solved. The structure is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I need to stay calm. I've delivered babies before. Well, I've read about delivering babies. Okay, I've seen pictures of babies being delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I need to be confident, reassuring, medically trained, emotionally available, physically strong, and mentally prepared.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I need to know CPR, comfort techniques, pain management strategies, and emergency protocols.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I need to be like a doctor, a nurse, a midwife, a therapist, and... and my mom.

jokes.text: The Dean, mid-crisis, tells the journalist: 'Well, a lot more [babies] are conceived [in classrooms]. No, Paul, that's off the record and not true. Sort of.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is trying to spin the emergency for the journalist while the birth happens
jokes.punchline: He undermines his own retraction with 'sort of,' implying there's a known history of classroom conceptions at Greendale
jokes.explanation: 'Not true. Sort of.' is a perfect two-word undercutting of his own retraction. The 'sort of' opens an enormous implication about Greendale's history. The sequence of 'off the record and not true. Sort of.' in rapid succession is good comedic architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: My grandfather, he was born during a flood. His mother gave birth in a tree.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: My other grandfather, he was born during an earthquake. The midwife had to deliver him while hanging from a rope.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: But my great-grandfather? He was born while his father was eating soup. And his father refused to put the soup down. So the midwife had to work around the soup bowl. He never even looked up from his meal.

jokes.text: Annie panics about delivering the baby: 'I can't deliver a baby. I'm not properly prepared. I need to take a class, or read a book, or shadow a nurse, or at least have my mom hug me first.'
jokes.setup: Abed has just told Annie she'll need to deliver the baby
jokes.punchline: Annie's escalating list of preparation requirements ends with the most childlike and emotionally honest request: a hug from her mom
jokes.explanation: The escalation from reasonable ('take a class') to increasingly infantile ('have my mom hug me first') is a perfect character joke. Annie's type-A anxiety and underlying emotional fragility are both in here. The list structure builds well and the final item is the right note to end on.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You care so much about people, you literally vomit empathy.

jokes.text: Jeff tries to calm Shirley down with 'Look at my face. Connect with me.' — and apparently breaks into some kind of singing or performance [14:00]: 'What in the hell?' / 'I don't know what to do!'
jokes.setup: Jeff confidently takes charge of calming Shirley, instructing her to 'connect' with him
jokes.punchline: Whatever Jeff does causes Shirley to react with 'What in the hell?' — implying his calming strategy is bizarre or alarming
jokes.explanation: The joke is primarily visual/performance-based — Jeff's self-confident 'connect with me' implies he has a specific calming technique, but it clearly goes wrong. 'What in the hell?' as the reaction and 'I don't know what to do!' from Annie suggests Jeff's method is alarming. This would read much better on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Listen up everyone, we need to work together right now. This is about survival.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I know, Jeff. Being a mother is the ultimate survival instinct. We're all just trying to nurture and protect—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Britta, what are you talking about? There's an active fire in the building!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Right, and mothers deal with fires all the time. Metaphorically speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is literally not about motherhood at all.

jokes.text: Chang reassures Shirley with stories of Chang babies surviving impossible conditions: 'My cousin slid out feet-first in a pickle barrel. My uncle was born during rainy season in a Mongolian sheep pasture. My brother, born under a crowded noodle bar while my grandfather finished his happy dancing shrimp.'
jokes.setup: Chang is asked to comfort Shirley with stories of Chang hardiness
jokes.punchline: Three escalating birth locations, each more specific and improbable, culminating in 'grandfather finished his happy dancing shrimp' — implying perfect Chang indifference to emergency
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The three-beat structure is perfect: pickle barrel → Mongolian sheep pasture → noodle bar while grandfather finishes his meal. Each escalates in specificity. 'Happy dancing shrimp' as the specific dish grandfather wouldn't put down is the ideal detail. The implication that the grandfather prioritized his shrimp dish over the birth of his son is devastating and hilarious. This is an 8-9 range joke in craft and impact.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's like a bus. Once it starts moving, you just have to let it go where it needs to go. You can't steer a bus.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not comforting.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm not trying to comfort you. I'm trying to explain obstetrics.

jokes.text: Chang: 'Nothing can stop us. Not the hurricanes. Not the communists. Not the feds. Not the girl scouts.'
jokes.setup: Chang is on a roll about Chang invincibility
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from natural disasters to political enemies to federal law enforcement to — the Girl Scouts, implying a specific ongoing conflict with the Girl Scouts
jokes.explanation: The list structure escalates perfectly, and the Girl Scouts as the final entry is an inspired choice — they're the most benign adversary imaginable, yet clearly a genuine threat to the Changs. 'Not the girl scouts' implies a specific, unresolved conflict that the audience will never learn about and is funnier for it. This is excellent economy — each item is one breath. The callback to this line later ('Not the girl scouts. Not the--') elevates it further. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The bus drives itself.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going to need you to explain that metaphor, because the implications are getting increasingly uncomfortable.

jokes.text: Jeff's pep talk to Britta concludes: 'Look, Britta, there is something in you that wants to take care of people so bad that you'll do it until you puke.' Britta: 'Are you saying I'll be a good mom?' Jeff: 'What? No.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is motivating Britta to deliver the baby by identifying her actual caring nature
jokes.punchline: Britta's attempt to extract maternal validation from a clinical observation is immediately shut down. Jeff is bewildered she went there.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's pep talk is a classic 'you'll do it until you puke' backhanded compliment — not exactly inspiring, but accurate. Britta reaching for 'will I be a good mom?' from this is a revealing character moment. Jeff's flat 'What? No.' is perfectly calibrated. Good structure, strong character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You think that's bad? My children lived underground like mole people for years. They developed their own language, their own currency. When we finally dug them out, they didn't even remember what the sun was.

jokes.text: Britta declares: 'Step aside, people! Britta for the win!'
jokes.setup: Britta has been talked into delivering the baby after initially panicking
jokes.punchline: Britta goes from zero to maximum confidence in an instant, declaring herself the winner before anything has happened
jokes.explanation: 'Britta for the win' is a solid character moment — her overcorrection from panic to bravado is very Britta. It's not a complex joke but it's well-delivered and character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I can do this. This is it. This is what I'm meant to do. I'm a doula. I'm a birth coach. This is my calling.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Ma'am, we're trained professionals—

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Not as trained as I am in this moment. Step aside.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Step aside, people! Britta for the win!' — immediately followed by her returning and saying 'Not the girl scouts. Not the--' before getting back to work
jokes.setup: Britta has been motivated to deliver the baby and enters with a dramatic announcement
jokes.punchline: She's still reciting Chang's speech as she gets into position — a callback that reveals she was actually moved by the Chang mythology
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Britta's 'Britta for the win!' is funny in its self-aggrandizement, and the detail that she's still reciting Chang's speech shows she took it to heart. The cut-off mid-phrase ('Not the girl scouts. Not the--') is perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: The baby's here! It's a beautiful baby girl, and she's... she's black.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Not that there's anything wrong with that! I mean, obviously not. That's great. She's perfect. I just wanted to point it out so nobody else had to, awkwardly, later.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Man, you will really force anything, won't you?' then immediately: 'Just get in there and force that baby out of Shirley.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just criticized Britta for forcing an interpretation; he needs her to act
jokes.punchline: He immediately uses the word 'force' in its literal physical sense, creating an unintentional parallel to his insult
jokes.explanation: Jeff catches himself using 'force' in both a critical and literal sense within the same breath, and the juxtaposition is funny. 'Force that baby out of Shirley' is also just a funny sentence to say with authority. The self-undermining wordplay works efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So the baby's not mine?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Thank God. Do you know what this means? It means I don't have to pass on the Chang tail.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: We've had tails for generations.

jokes.text: Abed to Britta on the difficulty of delivery: 'Don't tell any doctors I said this, but at this point in time, the bus pretty much drives itself.' Britta: 'Who exactly is the bus in this scenario?'
jokes.setup: Britta asks what she needs to do; Abed wants to minimize her anxiety
jokes.punchline: Abed uses a metaphor carelessly, and Britta—in the middle of an emergency—stops to ask for clarification about the metaphor's referent
jokes.explanation: Britta stopping mid-labor-delivery to question the structural integrity of Abed's metaphor is very true to her character — her anxious pedantry emerges at the worst moment. It's also a good joke about Abed's sometimes poorly-calibrated communication. Good character work for both.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I missed this.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Me too.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Ready?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Always.

jokes.text: Britta: 'I am nailing this! You're doing great too.' (to Shirley, while praising herself first)
jokes.setup: Britta is mid-delivery and reporting the progress
jokes.punchline: She leads with self-congratulation before remembering to compliment Shirley, the one actually in labor
jokes.explanation: Perfect Britta character joke. Her self-congratulation ('I am nailing this!') coming before acknowledging Shirley ('You're doing great too') is completely in character — her good intentions are always mediated through self-focus. The 'too' is what makes it.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm prepared to make a formal statement. While I maintain that this baby is not biologically mine, I'm willing to concede this point in the interest of maintaining harmony within our study group. I think you'll all agree that this kind of magnanimity is the mark of a true leader.

jokes.text: Chang's World War II Chang baby story: 'hundreds of Changs were born underneath the earth. Most spent their first five years underground.'
jokes.setup: Chang is continuing to provide motivational birth stories during the delivery
jokes.punchline: The WWII labor camp story pivots from historical horror to the detail that the babies spent five years underground, presented as a point of pride
jokes.explanation: Chang treating serious historical trauma as evidence of Chang baby toughness is consistently funny. The image of babies spending five years underground as a flex is dark and specific. The Chang mythology gag continues to pay off.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: We could name him Ben, after you, Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Ben Chang? That's perfect!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Actually, his last name is Bennett.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Ben Bennett? Ben... Bennett?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: It has a nice alliteration.

jokes.text: Baby is born. Britta announces: 'It's baby Greendale.' Abed: 'You guys don't have to name it that. I don't claim that power. I'm merely the deliverer.'
jokes.setup: The baby has just been born and Britta names it after the school
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately disclaims any naming authority despite having guided the delivery, with oddly specific humility
jokes.explanation: 'I don't claim that power. I'm merely the deliverer.' is a funny line — Abed has an unusually clear sense of his own role boundaries. His disclaimer is oddly formal and self-aware. Britta naming the baby after the school is also a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Did you hear that? The baby said 'Chang!' The baby said my name!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's just baby noises, Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.line: Yeah man, it didn't say anything.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No no no, it was definitely 'Chang!' I heard it clear as day!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Chang, please.

dialogue.speaker: Andre
dialogue.line: Let it go, buddy.

jokes.text: Shirley gives birth to a boy. Troy immediately announces: 'And it's also a black person! Not that that's important.'
jokes.setup: The baby's birth is announced and everyone is processing its existence
jokes.punchline: Troy announces the baby's race as a fact, then immediately disclaims its importance — but the disclaimer implies he was specifically noting it to settle the paternity question
jokes.explanation: Troy's delivery is perfect — the announcement that it's 'also a black person' (the 'also' implying he was processing multiple new facts simultaneously), followed by the reflexive 'not that that's important,' settles the Chang paternity plot without anyone having to say it directly. The fact that it IS important is entirely communicated by Troy trying to say it isn't. Excellent economy and social comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We just watched a human being come into the world. And it was miraculous. But you know what the miracle really is? That any of us survive it. I mean, we start out as literally nothing—just some cells dividing in the dark. And then nine months later, we're forced through a biological meat grinder, covered in fluids we don't want to think about. And somehow, we make it. We survive. And then we spend the rest of our lives thinking we're special.

jokes.text: Chang insists on one final bid at paternity: 'I never told you this part, but all Changs are born with tails. You kind of dodged a bullet there.'
jokes.setup: The baby is confirmed as Andre's; Chang's paternity claims are over
jokes.punchline: Chang concedes gracefully but adds that Chang babies have tails — framing Shirley's relief as luck
jokes.explanation: Chang's concession speech includes 'you kind of dodged a bullet there' regarding Chang tails — it's both a gracious exit from the paternity claim and a final flex. The Chang mythology continues to build. 'All Changs are born with tails' as a revealed detail this late in the episode is perfect timing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Are we destined for greatness?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Of course we are. I mean, look at me. The way I just delivered that line? That's greatness.

jokes.text: Pierce/Troy note that the Troy/Abed handshake 'came back' — 'It's back.' / 'It never left.'
jokes.setup: The handshake had been 'ruined' by Pierce's purchase; now after witnessing the birth, it spontaneously returns
jokes.punchline: Abed's 'It never left' implies the magic of the handshake is about the relationship, not the act — a small emotional note delivered with Abed's characteristic deadpan
jokes.explanation: The B-plot resolution is handled beautifully — 'It never left' is Abed at his most emotionally precise. It's both a logical closing statement (the bond wasn't contingent on the gesture) and unexpectedly touching. Good economy — four words to close an episode-long subplot. Rewatch bonus for seeing it in context of the full arc.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Look at those tiny fingers. They're like little candy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I kind of want to eat them.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's lame.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Chang: 'Congratulations, sir. After a fierce campaign, I happily concede this baby to you. Pretty classy of me.'
jokes.setup: Andre has arrived and Chang needs to acknowledge his paternity
jokes.punchline: Chang frames his retreat as a 'concession' in an election-style campaign, then congratulates himself on his own class
jokes.explanation: Chang treating the paternity dispute as an election campaign with a concession speech is perfectly in character — his grandiosity and self-congratulation ('pretty classy of me') are core Chang traits. The formal register of 'I happily concede' is funny in context.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Finally! Positive coverage! This is it! This is my moment!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm going to be remembered! I'm going to be a legend!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Greendale's greatest leader! The Dean of Dreams!

jokes.text: Shirley names the baby Ben Bennett. Chang: 'Ben Bennett? Oh, damn. Okay. No, no. No, that's fine. Ben Bennett. Hi, Ben Bennett.'
jokes.setup: Shirley wants to honor Chang by naming the baby Ben; Chang is touched — until he hears the full name
jokes.punchline: Ben Bennett is a terrible name, and Chang's real-time processing of this realization — from touched to disappointed to resigned — is the joke
jokes.explanation: Chang's emotional journey from 'What?' (hopeful) to 'Really?' to 'Oh, damn.' to 'No, that's fine' in four beats is a compressed comedic arc. His attempt to make peace with 'Ben Bennett' by just saying it out loud twice doesn't work — he can hear how bad it is. Well-structured reaction comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We know about your fake anthropology class, Duncan.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We have evidence. Photos. Emails. We're going to the Dean unless you cancel school tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We've learned a lot at Greendale. Turns out blackmail is just applied networking.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Plus, we learned it from watching you.

jokes.text: Chang insists the baby said 'Chang.' No one agrees. 'See? Nothing to it.'
jokes.setup: The newborn makes a sound; Chang interprets it as saying his name
jokes.punchline: Everyone denies it; Chang moves on with 'See? Nothing to it' — suggesting he has concluded the successful legacy of his Chang-ness in the child
jokes.explanation: A small coda gag. Chang's interpretation of baby sounds as 'Chang' is consistent with his self-mythology. 'See? Nothing to it' is a nice non-sequitur exit line. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Jeff reflects: 'Can you believe that's how we come into this world? Screaming, crying, covered in crap?' Britta: 'And then somewhere along the lines, we get it into our heads that we're destined for greatness.' Jeff: 'We are. I just yanked a little dude out of my friend.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta share a reflective moment after the birth
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds to Britta's philosophical observation with literal pride in what just happened, using 'little dude' and 'yanked' to deflate the sentiment
jokes.explanation: 'I just yanked a little dude out of my friend' as a statement of greatness is a nice landing for the episode's emotional arc. It's simultaneously sincere and absurd — 'yanked' and 'little dude' are the right deflationary word choices for Jeff to use while actually feeling something.

jokes.text: Annie, looking at the baby's hands: 'His fingers are like Good & Plenties.' Shirley: 'I know. I want to eat them.' Annie: 'Which is lame.' Shirley: 'Totally.'
jokes.setup: Annie and Shirley are cooing over the new baby's tiny fingers
jokes.punchline: The sweet moment of baby-worship is immediately self-aware — Shirley's desire to eat the fingers and Annie's reflexive 'which is lame' / Shirley's 'totally' agreement creates a funny loop of sincere emotion and self-consciousness
jokes.explanation: 'Like Good & Plenties' is a funny specific candy comparison for tiny fingers. The 'I want to eat them / which is lame / totally' exchange is a nice rhythm — the characters catch themselves being sentimental and choose to mock it even while being sentimental.

jokes.text: The journalist promises a cover story 'in a good way.' Dean: 'Like an article about what a good dean I am?' Journalist: 'Absolutely.' [Cut] Dean alone: 'I did it. I did it. I am a good dean. I AM A GOOD DEAN! WHOO!'
jokes.setup: The Dean has been anxiously managing his image for Dean Magazine all episode; the journalist seems to approve
jokes.punchline: The Dean allows himself a full private victory celebration that escalates from quiet self-confirmation to screaming triumph — suggesting this validation means everything to him
jokes.explanation: The Dean's escalating self-affirmation is a perfect character payoff. 'I did it. I did it. I am a good dean. I AM A GOOD DEAN! WHOO!' reads like a man convincing himself with increasing conviction — the repetition is key. It's both pathetic and joyful, which is the Dean's whole deal. The escalation from whisper to scream is implied by the capitalization and punctuation. High character integration.

jokes.text: Jeff and Troy are in the hallway, clearly about to blackmail the Dean. Troy: 'Are you sure you want to do this? I know people do it in movies all the time, but there are bound to be real world consequences.' Jeff: 'I know, but if we take that test today, we are definitely going to fail it.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Troy are outside the Dean's office, contemplating something serious — the buildup sounds like they might be about to do something genuinely consequential
jokes.punchline: The only real-world consequence they're managing is failing a test — their moral deliberation is entirely self-serving and petty
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom misdirection — solemn deliberation about a 'real world consequence' deflated by the revelation that the consequence is just failing Duncan's already-fake test. The moral weight they're applying to test avoidance is funny.

jokes.text: Jeff and Troy enter the Dean's office. Long pause [19:21-19:28]. Then: 'Cancel school today or we tell everybody about this.' Dean: 'Deal.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Troy are about to blackmail the Dean; we don't know what they have on him
jokes.punchline: Whatever they've discovered (never shown to the audience) is so immediately compromising that the Dean folds without negotiation — and the audience never learns what it is
jokes.explanation: One of the best structural jokes in the episode and perhaps the best closer. Community withholds the visual punchline entirely — we see the approach, we hear 'Deal,' and we never learn what the Dean was doing. The Dean's instant capitulation is funnier than any reveal could be, because the audience's imagination fills it with something worthy of his immediate surrender. This is craft-forward comedy — the joke is in what's NOT shown. High structural originality; economy is near-perfect.

tmdb_overview: As the semester ends, the anthropology final is disrupted when Shirley goes into labor and her husband, Andre, is summoned to school for the birth.
insight: Season finale delivers 68 jokes in 22 minutes—Community's densest episode to date.
